books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Senator Blanche K. Bruce, speech before the Senate (March 31, 1876)

stimulus.text:
“I have confidence, not only in this country and her institutions, but in the endurance, capacity, and destiny of my people. We will, as opportunity offers and ability serves, seek our places, sometimes in the field of letters, arts, sciences, and the professions. More frequently mechanical pursuits will attract and elicit our efforts; more still of my people will find employment and livelihood as the cultivators of the soil. The bulk of this people—by surroundings, habits, adaption, and choice—will continue to find their homes in the South, and constitute the masses of its yeomanry.”

—Senator Blanche K. Bruce, speech before the Senate to introduce a resolution appointing a committee to investigate election practices in Mississippi, March 31, 1876
stimulus.source_note: Senator Blanche K. Bruce, speech before the Senate, March 31, 1876. Public domain. Wording verified against the quotation in 5 Steps to a 5, AP U.S. History 2024, Chapter 16, including the book’s spelling “adaption.”

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Bruce could speak with confidence about his people’s future mainly because Reconstruction had

options.text: given every freed family forty acres of land.
options.misconception: Background: no law gave freed families forty acres, and Bruce never claims it did.

options.text: made Black men citizens and voters, and sent them to Congress.
ended all violence against Black Southerners.
options.misconception: Background: violence against Black Southerners was rising in 1876, and Bruce was speaking about election violence.

options.text: made the South’s economy richer than the North’s after the war.
options.misconception: Background: the South’s economy was wrecked by war, not richer than the North’s.

rationales.A: Background: no law gave freed families forty acres, and Bruce never claims it did.
rationales.B: Bruce himself was the proof: a Black man from Mississippi, sitting in the United States Senate. The amendments had made Black men citizens and voters, and Reconstruction had sent them to statehouses and to Congress.
rationales.C: Background: violence against Black Southerners was rising in 1876, and Bruce was speaking about election violence.
rationales.D: Background: the South’s economy was wrecked by war, not richer than the North’s.
rationales.general:
1. Bruce is speaking in the Senate, as a senator from Mississippi, about his own people.
2. Background: ten years earlier, Black men could not vote, hold office, or testify in Southern courts.
3. The amendments changed that, and Bruce’s seat is the evidence sitting in front of his audience.
4. His confidence rests on a change he embodies.
Remember: when a speaker is living proof of the change, the change is the answer.
